explanation: Fires on mid-word subword tokens in personal names inside email addresses in copyright headers (e.g. 'Fl[orian]'.Rival@gmail), strongest there; also fires moderately on word-internal subword pieces and function words in non-English text (German, Norwegian/Danish, Hungarian, Turkish, Somali, Hindi), including closing quotes in German/Dutch news. Weak on ordinary English.

Fires on a token early in a document, just after a heading, title or boilerplate opener (e.g. 'Monthly [Archives]', 'Publication [history]', 'The [present] invention', 'DO NOT [MODIFY]', 'Here['s]' right after a Q: title). What matters is position at the start of a new section or document, not the token's identity; there is no clear lexical pattern.

Fires most strongly on 'subject' in PHP license headers ('This source file is [subject] to the ... license'). Elsewhere it fires moderately on a wide mix of tokens (word completions like 'Cauchy-Sch[warz]', 'Escarp[ment]', code identifiers, modal verbs) with no shared theme.

Moderate, diffuse activations on tokens in technical or code contexts (Elixir/Go code, ssl/keytool, lab methods like 'immunoblot [using]', 'blots [with]'), plus scattered prepositions. Only one strong example ('{_, pid} [=]' in Elixir); no coherent concept.

Fires on words in phrases that say something is wrong or happening for unclear reasons: 'something [is] wrong', 'what am I [doing] wrong', 'what is [going] on', 'something [was] happening', '[Something] went wrong'. Strongest on the verb or 'something' just before 'wrong' or 'happening'. Weaker on biomedical descriptions of abnormal function.

Fires most on 'at' in the Apache license boilerplate 'You may obtain a copy of the License [at]', just before a URL. It also fires strongly on a heterogeneous set of other tokens: '$this->[db]', the opening quote of a URL string, decimals in numbers, subword completions of journal names (Geosc[ience], Micro[be]) and citation pieces.

Fires on stock words in license and auto-generated-code headers: 'Licensed [under]', 'Apache [License]', 'under the [terms] of the GNU', 'This code was [generated]', 'DO NOT EDIT'. It also fires on similar formulaic phrases in awards and legal text ('Award for [Outstanding]', 'Player [of] the Year', 'ineffective ass[istance]') and on 'bibli[ography]' in metadata.

Fires on a mixed set: the minus sign starting the second equation in algebra word problems (', [-]2*l'), 'pro [se]' in legal text, items in code strings (bcrypt '$2a[$]', button('[loading]'), '[step]'), and assorted content words. No shared feature.

Fires on prepositions and articles in Portuguese and French text ('[no] time', 'remise [en]', '[en] 2019') and on the first subword of proper names in lists ('[Som]erville', '[Mon]rovia', '[Carlo] Maratta'). It also fires on version-number dots in build files and on list items. No single theme.
Fires very strongly only on a '0' token inside a long run of zeros (e.g. '0000000000[0]5313'). Essentially nothing else gets above about 2% of max.

Fires on separators and numbers inside reference IDs and numbering: the hyphen in patent and application numbers ('2014[-]2011', 'Soh 66[-]4709'), digits in citation anchors ('#mrm[2]7594', '{#sec[1]}'), journal-ID pieces and log PIDs. It also fires moderately on assorted subword completions.

Fires on capitalized proper nouns and named entities, especially politically charged or brand names (Comey, Kardashians, Oculus, NASCAR, Obamacare, AFC Wimbledon, NUnit) and on legal terms ('Code of [Civil] Procedure', 'misdemeanor'). It also fires on 'c[eliac]' and a broken Hindi byte; the token itself matters most.

Fires on the word linking a person or fact to the media outlet or organization it is attributed to: 'featured on USA Today[,]', 'staff writer [for]', '[told] Gazzetta', 'interview [with]', 'polled [by] Reuters', 'developer [at] BuzzFeed'. Strongest when a publication name follows; weaker for generic 'according [to]'.

Fires on an 'l' or '-l' token, often an OCR misreading of '1' or a lowercase 'l' starting a broken word: contract numbers ('HTC71[ l]', 'W5J9JE[-l]'), chemistry prefixes ('[-l]abeled', '[-l]-homocysteine', 'a [l]ipoxygenase'), '21[-l]bs'. Strongest on OCR-garbled IDs in legal documents.
